8694-the-abbot-s-ghost-or-maurice-treher:
A. M. Barnard, a pen name of Louisa May Alcott, wrote this 1867 Christmas story about Maurice Treherne and the ghost said to haunt an old abbey. The tale opens in a country house at Christmas, where Frank and a major trade jokes by the fire, one calling the lovely Octavia the worm the early bird catches. Beneath the festive talk sits anxiety, sharp glances, and a secret someone is guarding.

Temptation, a disputed inheritance, and a haunting drive the plot, as Treherne faces a choice between honour and gain. Alcott, writing sensational tales under a pseudonym while building her reputation for domestic fiction, lets the ghost story carry a moral sting. Readers who know her only from Little Women will find a darker, livelier Alcott here, spinning a winter mystery with a conscience at its centre.
doe-osti-3023107-securing-the-modern-gri:
Report INL/RPT-25-89606, dated November 2025, comes from Idaho National Laboratory staff Megan Culler and Remy Stolworthy with Patrick Heeter, Alex Tylecote, Todd Ponto, Josh Kmiec, and Luke Martin of ScottMadden, Inc. Grid expansion and modernization are underway across the United States, backed by state and federal money. The authors ask whether security and supply chain planning are keeping pace with the build-out.

Federal support is pushing advanced metering, AI-powered analytics, battery storage, and distributed energy management into the grid, turning one-way delivery into a responsive network. Against that gain, the report weighs supply chain exposure, including foreign rules on vulnerability disclosure that can hand adversaries early knowledge of weaknesses. Strategy sections tie investment choices to those risks.
doe-osti-3362527-frequency-nadir-constra:
Xuebo Liu presents this award-winning slide set, dated January 29, 2026, with Xin Fang, Ningchao Gao, and colleagues from the National Laboratory of the Rockies, Kansas State, and Mississippi State. The paper behind it won a best paper honor in the IEEE Open Access Journal of Power and Energy. Island grids lose inertia as solar and wind inverters replace spinning generators, so a single outage can drop frequency fast and deep, toward forced load shedding.

The fix bakes a floor on the frequency dip, the nadir, straight into unit commitment scheduling. Without any inertia floor, the studied island grid hit zero inertia about 10 percent of the year. A fixed floor forced 13.7 percent solar curtailment and still missed full safety. The tuned case saved about 13 million dollars a year and cut curtailment by 58 percent.
doe-osti-3363540-investigation-of-encaps:
Mimi C. Yung of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory reports for 2025 on encapsulin protein shells as scaffolds for making biomaterials. The work uses Rhodococcus bacteria. The annual report is dated April 30, 2026. Postdoctoral researcher Wei Li carried much of the bench work. These tiny shells can gather the steps of a production pathway in one place. That raises reaction efficiency.

The year's work included a forward genetic screen in the team's reporter strain. Cells carried a fluorescent marker gene. They grew under repressing and inducing conditions. A flow sorter then picked out odd cells. Mutants whose glow differed clearly from the parent strain became candidates for sequencing. The screen hunts the genes that control shell production.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-JusticeDepartme:
A legal memorandum examines the effect of Weisberg v. Department of Justice on another case, Center for National Policy Review v. Weinberger, in the D.C. Circuit, number 73-1090. Harold Weisberg's records suits made law that other litigants then had to reckon with. The memo works out what his precedent meant inside a live appeal.

Freedom of Information law was built case by case in this era, and Weisberg built more of it than most. A memo tracing his case's effect shows doctrine moving from one courtroom to another. The analysis preserves lawyers reading Weisberg the way later requesters would read them.
the-abbot-s-ghost-or-maurice-treherne-s-:
A. M. Barnard wrote The Abbot's Ghost, or Maurice Treherne's Temptation, as a Christmas story in 1867. Chapter one, headed Dramatis Personae, opens with talk before a fire in a grand house at the start of a holiday visit.

Frank and the Major trade barbs about lovely Octavia, the prize both men may seek, while fresh guests roll up by carriage. General Snowdon and his wife arrive, and Maurice Treherne has come while the men were out. The Major calls his case a hard one, and Frank presses for the facts before dinner. Readers get a country-house Christmas tale with a ghost, a crippled heir, and love crossed by pride and a dark house secret.
